title: Performing the unspoken: Protocol for an ethnodrama study of caregiver burden among Arab migrant women caring for older adults at home in the Greater Toronto Area
content:
by Areej Al-Hamad, Yasin M. Yasin, Kateryna Metersky, Kristina Kokorelias, Cole Lewis

Informal caregiving enables many older adults to remain at home, yet the work of family caregivers is often poorly recognized and unevenly supported. Among Arab migrant women, caregiving may be shaped by strong traditions of family responsibility, gendered expectations, migration and settlement pressures, language barriers, employment and childcare responsibilities, and limited access to culturally responsive services. This protocol describes a one-year, three-phase, arts-based community-engaged study developed in partnership with the Arab Community Centre of Toronto (ACCT). The study is guided by Ethics of Care and Intersectionality frameworks and aims to understand the caregiving realities of Arab migrant women who support older adults at home in the Greater Toronto Area (GTA), Canada, translate their narratives into ethnodrama, and co-generate actionable recommendations for community and service systems. Phase 1 will use qualitative descriptive methods and purposive sampling to conduct approximately 20–25 semi-structured interviews with such women aged 18 years or older who currently provide, or have recently (last 5 years) provided, unpaid care to an older adult at home in the GTA. Interviews will examine caregiving roles, emotional and social burden, cultural and family expectations, migration and settlement, employment and childcare, service access, coping, resilience, and support needs. Data will be analyzed using thematic analysis. Phase 2 will use Saldaña-informed ethnodramatic methods to adapt de-identified, composite interview excerpts into four short scenes portraying key caregiving experiences. Draft scripts will be reviewed with the participants with attention to confidentiality and participant comfort, rehearsed and performed with drama students, and screened in community, academic, and online settings. Anonymous audience reflections and facilitated post-performance dialogue will generate additional data on awareness, empathy, caregiver needs, and culturally responsive supports. Phase 3 will use two virtual Nominal Group Technique sessions with approximately 10–15 caregivers, community members, service providers, and stakeholders to generate, clarify, rank, and prioritize practical recommendations. Findings across phases will be integrated to produce multi-level recommendations, a community report, ethnodrama-based knowledge mobilization outputs, academic publications, and a hybrid knowledge mobilization summit. The study is designed to make often-unspoken caregiving experiences of vulnerable caregivers visible while protecting participant confidentiality and generating community-relevant evidence for culturally responsive caregiver support.
